stories.title: Reopen my last policy sources and show everything on start
stories.what: When the program starts, my remembered preferences, the policy sources I used last and their comments are brought back, and the list of policies opens on the broadest view, user and computer policies together.
stories.why: I get back to the policy work where I left it without choosing anything again, and a problem with remembering never stops me.

terms.name: Policy source
terms.means: Where policies are read from and saved to, such as the local Group Policy, a policy file, the registry or a scratch space; it is not the definitions that describe the policies.

criteria.says: Given the program's remembered preferences cannot be kept, when the program starts, then it carries on with the defaults, my changes to preferences are dropped, and I am not told, so nothing is remembered between runs.
Given I have never saved policy sources, when the program starts for the first time, then both the user source and the computer source open as the local Group Policy.

Given the policy sources I saved last time cannot be opened, when the program starts, then I am told "The previous policy sources are not accessible. The defaults will be loaded.", both sources are reset to the local Group Policy and opened without any further message; only the kind of source is reset and any saved location text stays.

Given a source has a place to keep comments, when the program opens it, then its existing comments are brought back, a missing comment file simply means no comments yet, and a source whose comments cannot be read is left without comments.
Given the program has started, when the list of policies is shown, then it is on "User or Computer", so user and computer policies appear together.

stories.title: Tell me once whether the workspace is ready to change
stories.what: After the sources open, one notice names the user and computer sources and says which are fully writable, which can only be viewed and which live only in memory.
stories.why: I know before I start whether my changes will be saved.

terms.name: Fully writable
terms.means: A source whose changes can be saved; not one that can only be viewed or that exists only in memory.

criteria.says: Given a source has just been opened, when the program works out whether I can change it, then a scratch space counts as writable, a registry source counts as not writable when saving a test value to it failed, and any other source counts as not savable when its file could not be opened for writing.

Given a source is described to me, when its state is shown, then it reads "is fully writable", "cannot be saved" (changes work in memory only) or "cannot be modified", and anything other than fully writable counts as a problem.

Given a source is named, when I see its name, then it is one of Local GPO, Registry, File, User GPO, User hive or Scratch space, followed in brackets by its location or the person's account identifier when it has one.

Given the sources have just opened, when either the user source or the computer source is not fully writable, then I am told "Not all policy sources are fully writable." together with the state of both; when both are fully writable, "Both the user and computer policy sources are loaded and writable." is shown only when opening was not quiet, so never when the program starts.

open: Which of "cannot be saved" and "cannot be modified" is shown for a registry source that failed its write test and which for a file source that could not be opened for writing?
Is the status bar name of a source also the name used in the readiness notice?

stories.title: Load the policy definitions I last used and recover from trouble
stories.what: At start the definitions from my saved folder, or the Windows default folder, are loaded; if there are problems I choose whether to keep a partly loaded set or fall back to the default location.
stories.why: The policies I can browse come from the definitions I trust, and a failed load is explained and recoverable.

terms.name: Policy definitions
terms.means: The templates that describe the available policies; not the sources where policy settings are stored.

criteria.says: Given a definitions folder was saved last time, when the program starts, then that folder is loaded; given none was saved, then the Windows default definitions folder is loaded.

Given loading the saved definitions reports problems, when I am asked whether to keep using the workspace, then Yes keeps the partly loaded workspace; No counts as a failed load with the reason "You decided to not use the problematic ADMX bundle.", the partly loaded workspace is thrown away, and what follows is the next two criteria.

Given the saved folder is not the Windows default and fails to load, when I am told "Policy definitions could not be loaded from "<folder>": <reason> Load from the default location?" (the reason is the problem found, or the "You decided..." reason after No), then Yes saves the Windows default folder as my definitions folder and No leaves the workspace empty with no further message.
Given I chose to load the default location, when it loads, then the workspace is replaced by an empty one and the Windows default folder is loaded into it.

Given the Windows default folder itself fails to load (including after I said No to keeping a partly loaded set from it), or fails to load after I chose Yes to the default location, when that happens, then I am told "Policy definitions could not be loaded: <reason>" and the workspace stays empty.
